Q: Plugin development for woocommerce : RFQ Broadcast Layer with Pincode Filtering A:

this is a well-scoped problem and your proposed architecture is largely on the right track.

A broadcast RFQ layer on top of Dokan is definitely buildable as a bridge plugin. The short answers to your questions: yes to CPT for RFQ cloning, yes to Action Scheduler for async processing at 50-100 vendor scale, and Dokan does expose hooks you can intercept cleanly without touching core.

The trickier parts are the vendor capability query (pincode matching gets messy with Dokan's geo implementation) and the comparison dashboard UX. Those tend to be where scope expands.

If you'd like to discuss the project further, feel free to reach out directly.

Q: How do I determine the state of a VBA workbook before attempting to close it (Excel 2007)? A:

Thanks for this, Tim. It appears to work. It boils down to the fact that you have been able to trap the <automation error> against wb.Name whereas I wasn't against wb on its own. Maybe it is something to do with the type. Here is a stripped down piece of code to show how it works with wb.Name

Const scPathFile as String = "C:\Dir\abc.xlsx"

dim s as string

dim wb as workbook

set wb = workbooks.Open(scPathFile)

wb.Close

On Error Resume Next

s = wb.name

wb.Close

s takes the value "". Without On Error Resume Next it throws an automation error when the workbook is not fully formed.

Q: django import-export foreignkey widget never called A: 
The custom widget is never instantiated because `modelresource_factory(model=Locality)()`
generates a fresh resource on the fly using default widgets - it doesn't use your
`LocalityResource` class with the custom `PlaceForeignKeyWidget`.

Use the explicit resource class instead:

`python
from crm.admin import LocalityResource  # adjust import path

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_locality_place_foreignkey():
    resource = LocalityResource()
    result = resource.import_data(dataset, dry_run=False)
    assert Locality.objects.count()`

Q: Using <input type=datetime-local> with <step> attribute to get intervals of 15 minutes A:

You have very specific needs, which I don't think can be easily accommodated with an input of type datetime-local. The min and max attributes refer to times at certain dates, not times for each day.

I also look at input of type time, but that won't work either. For instance, the drop down list is not supported in Firefox, and a drop down would be nice here.

Separate inputs for the dates and times would be, in my opinion, the best option here.

HTML can be verbose, especially when you have 50 lines of options, but I would not consider that bad practice.

You could generate the time options using Javascript:

const selector = document.getElementById("time");
const options = ["08:00", "08:15", "08:30", "08:45",
                 "09:00", "09:15", "09:30", "09:45",
                 "10:00", "10:15", "10:30", "10:45",
                 "11:00", "11:15", "11:30", "11:45",
                 "12:00", "12:15", "12:30", "12:45",
                 "13:00", "13:15", "13:30", "13:45",
                 "14:00", "14:15", "14:30", "14:45",
                 "15:00", "15:15", "15:30", "15:45",
                 "16:00", "16:15", "16:30", "16:45",
                 "17:00", "17:15", "17:30", "17:45",
                 "18:00"];

options.forEach((element, key) => {
  selector[key] = new Option(element, key);
});
<select id='time'>

But I'm not sure that is a real improvement. You could even try to generate the options array programmatically, but that will make it even more complex and difficult to understand. 50 lines of HTML is simpler. Shorter code isn't by definition better code.

An even more complex solution would be to fiddle with the values of a datetime-local input to exclude certain times, but I wouldn't bother. Two inputs will work just fine.
